title: The Relief Keeper
subtitle: Flannan Isles · Outer Hebrides, 1900
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, a remote Victorian lighthouse station on a steep rocky island in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland in December 1900, whitewashed stone, wet grey rock, heavy Atlantic sea, cold blue-grey winter light, melancholy and uncanny, period 1900 detail, cinematic vertical composition with one centred subject, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no legible writing, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: The ship fired a rocket. No one answered. The Flannan Isles lighthouse, in Scotland's Outer Hebrides. Boxing Day, nineteen hundred.
beats.img: A single bright red signal rocket trailing sparks high into a dark winter dusk sky above a small stone lighthouse on the summit of a steep rocky island, the lighthouse lantern dark and unlit, grey Atlantic swell below, the rocket and tower centred in the middle of the frame, no people.

beats.vo: The relief keeper, Joseph Moore, went ashore alone. He found the entrance gate closed. The outer door, closed.
beats.img: A closed iron entrance gate in a low whitewashed stone wall, a plain white lighthouse keepers' building with a shut wooden door behind it, wet flagstones, wind-flattened grass, heavy grey December sky, the gate centred in the frame, no people.

beats.vo: Inside, he wrote, the fire was not lighted for some days. The beds were empty, just as they left them in the early morning.
beats.img: A cold black cast-iron kitchen range in a plain Victorian lighthouse keepers' kitchen, grey dead ash in the open grate, no flame, an iron kettle on the hob, a scrubbed wooden table edge in the foreground, cold grey window light, the range centred in the frame, no people.

beats.vo: He did not search further. He wrote that he knew only too well something serious had occurred.
beats.img: Looking down a long steep stone stairway from a high rocky island toward a small concrete sea landing far below, a small dark steamship waiting offshore on a grey heaving sea, low winter cloud, the stairway running down the centre of the frame, no people.

beats.vo: That night, Moore and three men from the ship lit the light again. James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald McArthur were never found.
beats.img: A stone lighthouse tower on a dark rocky island at night, its lantern lit, a single pale beam reaching out over a black stormy Atlantic sea, the tower centred in the frame, rain in the air, lonely and unresolved, no people.

facts.claim: Flannan Isles lighthouse is on Eilean Mòr, Flannan Isles, Outer Hebrides, Scotland; the relief vessel Hesperus reached it on 26 December 1900 (Boxing Day)
The Hesperus fired a rocket (and sounded horn/whistle) on arrival and got no response — Master's telegram 26 Dec 1900: 'Fired a rocket but, as no response was made, managed to land Moore'
Joseph Moore, the relief keeper, was put ashore alone
Moore found the entrance gate closed and the (main) door closed — Moore's letter of 28 Dec 1900: 'on coming to the entrance gate I found it closed'
Moore's letter: 'the fire was not lighted for some days' (kitchen fireplace cold)
Moore's letter: 'found the beds empty just as they left them in the early morning'
Moore's letter: 'I did not take time to search further, for I only too well knew something serious had occurred'; he returned to the landing and reported to the ship
Moore 'lighted the light in the proper time that night and every night since'; the Master left Moore, the buoymaster and two seamen on the island 'to keep the light burning'
The three keepers were James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald McArthur; no trace of them was ever found
(caption) Moore's letter is dated 28 December 1900 (two days after landing) and went on public display for the first time in 2026 at the National Records of Scotland (exhibition 3 Aug–25 Sep 2026)
Still unexplained as of 2026: the June 2026 coverage of Moore's letter presents no new solution; families 'do not know for sure what happened'; official inquiry only inferred a large wave
